newsitem.title: USA: US Northeast temps seen moderating then cold again.
newsitem.headline: US Northeast temps seen moderating then cold again.

text.p: Temperatures in "the heating oil belt" of the U.S. Northeast will rise to above average this week and then turn below normal Friday through Monday, meteorologists said.
But, they said the cold snap will not be as severe as the one experienced this past weekend in the region, which is the largest heating oil market in the world.

"The arctic airmass does not look nearly as strong as the one during the past week, but it will send temperatures below normal levels across the eastern half of the nation for a three-to-four day period," said Jon Davis, meteorologist with Smith Barney in Chicago.
Davis expects temperatures to be five to 10 degrees above normal Wednesday and Thursday and then drop to an average of five to 10 degrees below normal Friday through Monday.
The near-term outlook of widely-read forecaster Weather Services Inc in Lexington, Mass. concurs with Davis's.

The reason the region will experience two cold spells consecutively is that the Northeast is being hit by an airmass delivered by the "Hudson Bay Vortex," a cold pattern circulating above the Hudson Bay in Canada, forecasters said.
"The nearer the vortex is to the U.S., the colder it will be (in the Northeast)," said Craig Solberg, forecaster with Freese-Notis Weather in Des Moines, Iowa.
Because the vortex's placement varies somewhat, this weekend could be colder than anticipated, Solberg said.
On the other hand, forecaster Fred Gesser of Weather Express Inc in Omaha, Neb. expects temperatures to be normal in the Northeast this weekend and then be above average next week.
"The vortex is becoming disorganized and diffuse," said Gesser.
The National Weather is expected to release an updated six to 10 day forecast later this evening.

Prices of heating oil futures have fallen three cents a gallon from last week on the New York Mercantile Exchange despite forecasts of cold this weekend and frigid weather last weekend. Dealers attribute the fall to supplies of heating oil being more than ample to meet demand.

According to the American Petroleum Institute's (API) oil inventory data for the week ended January 10, the year-over- year shortfall in distillate stocks, which are comprised of heating oil and diesel, has narrowed to 350,000 barrels from almost 20 million barrels in August.
((-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761))
